title: Transcription, Translation, Gene Regulation and Cancer — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Nucleic Acid Metabolism and Gene Expression and Regulation lectures (M. E. Annani-Akollor)

questions.stem: What biochemical product is created during transcription of a protein-coding gene?
questions.why: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase synthesizes an RNA strand complementary to its DNA template.

questions.stem: In what direction does RNA polymerase synthesize a growing RNA chain?

options.label: C
options.text: From both ends toward the middle

options.label: E
options.text: By ligating amino acids to bases

questions.why: RNA synthesis proceeds through 3′-OH attack on an incoming ribonucleoside triphosphate.

questions.stem: Why can RNA polymerase begin a transcript without the primer needed by DNA polymerase?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses DNA ligase as a primer

options.label: C
options.text: It initiates RNA synthesis de novo

options.label: D
options.text: It removes all DNA template bases

questions.why: RNA polymerases can initiate synthesis on a promoter-bound DNA template without a pre-existing RNA 3′ end.

questions.stem: Which DNA segment is most directly involved in specifying the site of transcription initiation?
questions.why: Promoter DNA recruits RNA polymerase and initiation factors near the transcription start site.

questions.stem: What is the function of the bacterial sigma factor during transcription initiation?
questions.why: Sigma helps bacterial RNA polymerase recognize promoter elements and start transcription.

questions.stem: Which sequence feature is characteristic of many bacterial promoters near the minus-ten position?
questions.why: The -10 TATAAT-like element is a major bacterial promoter recognition sequence.

questions.stem: Which general transcription factor contains TATA-binding protein for RNA polymerase II initiation?
questions.why: TFIID contains TBP, which recognizes TATA boxes in certain eukaryotic promoters.

questions.stem: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes most protein-coding messenger RNA?
questions.why: Pol II transcribes pre-mRNA and many regulatory RNAs.

questions.stem: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase primarily transcribes the large ribosomal RNA precursor?
questions.why: Pol I produces the 45S precursor of major rRNAs; Pol III transcribes 5S rRNA and many tRNAs.

questions.stem: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase commonly transcribes transfer RNA genes?
questions.why: Pol III synthesizes tRNA and 5S rRNA transcripts.

questions.stem: How does rho-dependent termination in bacteria stop RNA synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: A ribosome directly cleaves the DNA promoter

options.label: B
options.text: A spliced intron destroys RNA polymerase

options.label: D
options.text: An RNA-bound helicase releases the complex

options.label: E
options.text: Telomerase caps the growing RNA chain

questions.why: Rho is an ATP-driven RNA helicase that catches a paused polymerase and destabilizes the RNA–DNA hybrid.

questions.stem: Which drug directly inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase?
questions.why: Rifampicin targets the bacterial RNA polymerase beta subunit and inhibits transcription initiation.

questions.stem: Which toxin is especially potent against eukaryotic RNA polymerase II?
questions.why: Alpha-amanitin inhibits RNA polymerase II and thereby blocks mRNA synthesis.

questions.stem: What is the protective 5-prime cap added to many eukaryotic messenger RNAs?
questions.why: The 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap enhances mRNA stability, nuclear export and initiation of translation.

questions.stem: Which processing event removes introns and joins exons in eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
questions.why: snRNP-containing spliceosomes excise introns and ligate exons.

questions.stem: Why can a single gene produce multiple protein isoforms in different tissues?

options.label: E
options.text: Permanent conversion of RNA to DNA

questions.why: Alternative splicing selects different exon combinations in mature mRNA.

questions.stem: What is the main protective effect of the eukaryotic 3-prime poly-A tail?

options.label: C
options.text: Replacement of the mRNA coding frame

options.label: E
options.text: Direct initiation of ribosomal RNA synthesis

questions.why: The poly-A tail protects mRNA, influences stability and supports translation.

questions.stem: Which sequence on a mature tRNA accepts an activated amino acid?
questions.why: The terminal adenosine in the 3′ CCA acceptor arm carries the amino acid.

questions.stem: Which molecule catalyses peptide-bond formation in the ribosome?
questions.why: The peptidyl-transferase centre is formed primarily by ribosomal RNA, making the ribosome a ribozyme.

questions.stem: Which mRNA codon usually initiates translation and specifies methionine?
questions.why: AUG commonly serves as the start codon and encodes methionine or formylmethionine.

questions.stem: Which codon group functions as signals to terminate translation?
questions.why: UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons recognized by protein release factors.

questions.stem: What is the term for an mRNA triplet recognized by the complementary triplet of a tRNA?
questions.why: A codon specifies an amino acid or termination signal; its complementary tRNA sequence is the anticodon.

questions.stem: Why is the genetic code described as degenerate?

options.label: A
options.text: One codon always specifies two amino acids

options.label: C
options.text: Several codons can specify one amino acid

options.label: D
options.text: Each tRNA always binds all codons

options.label: E
options.text: There are only four total codons

questions.why: Many amino acids are encoded by more than one synonymous codon.

questions.stem: What determines the effect of inserting a single nucleotide inside a protein-coding region?

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate restoration of all amino acids

questions.why: An insertion not divisible by three changes codon grouping downstream, producing a frameshift.

questions.stem: What occurs when an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges its cognate tRNA?

options.label: A
options.text: An RNA intron is removed from DNA

options.label: B
options.text: An amino acid is linked to tRNA

options.label: C
options.text: A peptide is cleaved from a ribosome

options.label: E
options.text: A codon is transcribed into DNA

questions.why: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases use ATP to attach the correct amino acid to its matched tRNA.

questions.stem: Which ribosomal binding site holds the growing peptidyl-tRNA during elongation?
questions.why: The P site holds peptidyl-tRNA, the A site receives aminoacyl-tRNA and the E site permits exit.

questions.stem: What is the central dogma pathway for expression of a typical protein-coding gene?
questions.why: The ordinary information flow is transcription from DNA into RNA, followed by translation into protein.

questions.stem: Which bacterial DNA element serves as the binding site for a lac repressor?
questions.why: The lac repressor binds the operator, limiting transcription of the lactose-utilization structural genes.

questions.stem: What is the inducer-linked effect of lactose availability on the lac operon?

options.label: A
options.text: RNA polymerase cannot bind any promoter

options.label: B
options.text: The structural genes are irreversibly deleted

questions.why: Allolactose derived from lactose reduces repressor affinity for the operator, allowing transcription.

questions.stem: Which lac operon gene encodes beta-galactosidase?
questions.why: lacZ encodes beta-galactosidase, whereas lacY encodes permease and lacA encodes transacetylase.

questions.stem: Which lac operon gene encodes lactose permease?
questions.why: lacY encodes the transporter responsible for lactose entry.

questions.stem: Under which glucose condition does the cAMP–CAP activator most strongly enhance lac transcription?
questions.why: Low glucose raises cAMP, enabling CAP binding and positive regulation when lactose is available.

questions.stem: What is the direct role of tryptophan in repression of the trp operon?

options.label: A
options.text: It binds the lac permease directly

options.label: C
options.text: It acts as a repressor corepressor

questions.why: Tryptophan binds and activates the trp repressor, enabling operator binding when tryptophan is abundant.

questions.stem: What does attenuation regulate in the bacterial trp operon?
questions.why: Translation of a leader peptide influences RNA structures that control early transcription termination.

questions.stem: What is the usual effect of histone acetylation on nearby eukaryotic gene transcription?
questions.why: Acetylation neutralizes lysine charges and is generally associated with a more open transcriptionally active chromatin state.

questions.stem: What is the usual association of methylation at many gene-promoter CpG regions?
questions.why: Promoter CpG methylation often recruits transcriptional silencing mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which chromatin form is typically less condensed and relatively transcriptionally active?
questions.why: Euchromatin is generally open and accessible, unlike densely packed heterochromatin.

questions.stem: How can an enhancer influence transcription despite being far from the gene promoter?

options.label: A
options.text: It converts an intron into histone

options.label: D
options.text: It destroys the promoter DNA sequence

options.label: E
options.text: It changes amino acids in the gene

questions.why: Enhancer-bound regulatory proteins can interact with promoter complexes through DNA looping.

questions.stem: What is the advantage of combinatorial transcription-factor control in multicellular organisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Every cell must express all genes equally

options.label: B
options.text: All enhancers require one identical receptor

options.label: C
options.text: RNA polymerase loses all promoter specificity

options.label: D
options.text: Each hormone requires one single unique gene

questions.why: Cells integrate multiple transcriptional signals, enabling tissue-specific gene expression patterns.

questions.stem: Which mechanism changes the abundance of protein without changing transcription of its corresponding gene?
questions.why: Translation efficiency can vary independently of steady-state transcription.

questions.stem: Which process can lower steady-state protein concentration after the protein has already been synthesized?
questions.why: Targeted ubiquitination often directs proteins to the proteasome for degradation.

questions.stem: In iron deficiency, which change in ferritin expression helps conserve available iron?

options.label: C
options.text: Complete loss of ferritin coding DNA

questions.why: IRP binding to a 5′-UTR iron-responsive element inhibits ferritin translation when iron is scarce.

questions.stem: How is transferrin receptor mRNA commonly affected by iron deficiency?

options.label: E
options.text: Its protein is converted into ferritin

questions.why: IRP binding to 3′-UTR iron-responsive elements stabilizes transferrin receptor mRNA in low iron states.

questions.stem: Which alteration most directly converts a proto-oncogene into an oncogene?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of both copies of a tumour suppressor

options.label: B
options.text: Deletion of a DNA mismatch-repair gene

options.label: C
options.text: Irreversible silencing of normal growth genes

options.label: D
options.text: Increased degradation of a growth-factor receptor

options.label: E
options.text: An activating mutation or gene amplification

questions.why: Proto-oncogenes become oncogenes through gain-of-function changes such as activating mutations, gene amplification or abnormal expression.

questions.stem: Why can a gain-of-function mutation in one proto-oncogene allele promote tumorigenesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Both gene copies must first be deleted

options.label: B
options.text: One activated copy can drive signaling

options.label: C
options.text: Oncogenes work only after telomere loss

questions.why: Many oncogene gain-of-function variants are dominant at the cellular level.

questions.stem: What common pattern characterizes tumor-suppressor inactivation within a tumour cell?

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of both functional gene copies

questions.why: Many tumour suppressors follow a two-hit loss-of-function model, though exceptions occur.

questions.stem: Which transcription factor is commonly called the guardian of the genome?
questions.why: The TP53 product coordinates DNA-damage responses, cell-cycle arrest, senescence and apoptosis.

questions.stem: What is a direct benefit of p53-mediated cell-cycle arrest following DNA damage?

options.label: C
options.text: Time for DNA repair before division

questions.why: Checkpoint arrest permits cells to repair DNA or trigger apoptosis when damage is severe.

questions.stem: Which enzyme family executes much of the proteolysis during apoptosis?
questions.why: Initiator and executioner caspases cleave many cellular substrates during programmed cell death.

questions.stem: Which cellular change is more characteristic of apoptosis than uncontrolled necrosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of all plasma proteins before injury

options.label: E
options.text: Rapid diffusion of nuclear DNA from blood

questions.why: Apoptotic cells shrink and fragment into membrane-bound bodies, usually limiting inflammatory leakage.

questions.stem: What term describes spread of malignant cells to anatomically distant tissues?
questions.why: Metastasis involves invasion, dissemination, and colonization of a distant site.

questions.stem: Why must a growing solid tumour stimulate new blood vessel formation beyond a small size?

options.label: A
options.text: Diffusion alone cannot supply enough oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: Tumour cells have no mitochondrial proteins

options.label: C
options.text: Cancer cells cannot use any glucose

options.label: D
options.text: All malignant cells lose nuclear DNA

options.label: E
options.text: Tumour cells cease all protein synthesis

questions.why: Angiogenic signals such as VEGF help overcome diffusion limits on oxygen and nutrient supply.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a carcinogenic initiator and a tumour promoter?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiators activate antibodies; promoters destroy IgE

options.label: B
options.text: Initiators produce hormones; promoters make collagen

options.label: C
options.text: Initiators cause DNA lesions; promoters drive expansion

options.label: D
options.text: Initiators cause apoptosis; promoters repair DNA

options.label: E
options.text: Initiators block ribosomes; promoters form histones

questions.why: Initiators typically cause mutational damage; promoters foster proliferation or survival of initiated cells.

questions.stem: Which process most directly allows malignant cells to penetrate surrounding connective tissue?

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased cell motility at the border

questions.why: Invasive tumour cells change adhesion and degrade extracellular barriers to enter surrounding tissue.
